estimate: no NASA number for a suited walking slope was found; the patch itself (HiRISE at 1 m) is never steeper than 25 degrees, so 25 keeps every real slope walkable and steeper rock faces climbable only by the step row

estimate: no NASA number found; a heavy electric vehicle on loose ground reaching the SEV's ~2.8 m/s (10 km/h, https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/464826main_sev_factsheet_508.pdf) in 3 to 9 s

estimate: the SEV's wheels "pivot 360 degrees", so it can turn on the spot (https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/464826main_sev_factsheet_508.pdf); a slow pivot of 10 to 30 degrees a second, no measured rate found
estimate: a leaf or romaine lettuce head at harvest is commonly 20 to 35 cm across; the saved NASA Veggie paper (NTRS 20190028955) gives days to harvest, not size

Apollo crews 70 to 80+ steps a minute (https://www.nasa.gov/history/alsj/a11/a11.gaits.html); a suited 1 g treadmill study 88.8 steps/min (design/research/suit.md, Cullinane 2017). Value: walk speed / half the stride
two steps; Apollo 16 3.4 to 4.6 ft per stride (https://www.nasa.gov/history/alsj/a11/a11.gaits.html) and Cullinane 2017 1.243 m (design/research/suit.md); value = 1.0 m/s / 1.5 steps/s x 2
estimate: Apollo 16 fastest about 105 steps a minute (https://www.nasa.gov/history/alsj/a11/a11.gaits.html); no Mars-gravity measurement
peak knee flexion suited in reduced gravity, read off a graph (Norcross et al. 2010, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20110003409, Fig. 26): about 60 unsuited
feet apart while walking suited: Cullinane 2017 and Apollo 15 video (design/research/suit.md)
suited walk-to-run transition, Froude 0.36 +/- 0.11 over 38 Apollo gait events (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2719915/)
derived: 2 x 1.17 m/s / 3.73 m/s2, the Apollo 16 take-off speed under Mars gravity (see hero.jump.hop)

estimate: a foot counts as landed within 2 cm of the floor; a check on footstep timing, not a feel number

estimate: Armstrong on the Moon, 'I only go in a small fraction of an inch, maybe an eighth of an inch' (3 mm at 1/6 g; ALSJ 109:24:48, https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/static/history/alsj/a11/a11.step.html); Viking Lander 1 footpad 3 went 0.036 m into blocky ground (Moore et al. 1987, USGS PP 1389). A boot weighs 2.3 times as much on Mars (0.38 g against 0.166 g), so about 1 cm. Excerpts: design/research/pages/sinkage/excerpts.md
